questions.question: Q6. If a^4 + b^4 + c^4 = 2c^2*(a^2+b^2), prove that C = 45 deg or 135 deg. (T.U. 2051) (HSEB 2056)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q6 (T.U. 2051) (HSEB 2056); book pp187-188 = PDF p215 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: (b+c)^2 - a^2 = 3bc factors to b^2+c^2-a^2 = bc: read off cosA = 1/2.
questions.question: Q7. If (a+b+c)*(b+c-a) = 3bc, show that A = 60 deg.
questions.solution: (a+b+c)*(b+c-a) = (b+c)^2 - a^2 = b^2 + c^2 + 2bc - a^2. Setting this equal to 3bc gives b^2 + c^2 - a^2 = bc, so cosA = (b^2+c^2-a^2)/(2bc) = 1/2. With 0 < A < pi, A = 60 deg.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q7; book p188 = PDF p215 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Clear denominators: (a+c)+(b+c) over product form collapses to (a+b)^2 = c^2 + 3ab.
questions.question: Q8. If 1/(a+c) + 1/(b+c) = 3/(a+b+c), show that C = 60 deg. (T.U. 2054, HSEB 2053)
questions.solution: Combining: [(b+c) + (a+c)]/[(a+c)(b+c)] = 3/(a+b+c), i.e. (a+b+2c)(a+b+c) = 3[(a+c)(b+c)]. Put s1 = a+b: (s1+2c)(s1+c) = 3[c^2 + c*s1 + ab], i.e. s1^2 + 3c*s1 + 2c^2 = 3c^2 + 3c*s1 + 3ab, so s1^2 = c^2 + 3ab. Hence (a+b)^2 = c^2 + 3ab, i.e. a^2 + b^2 - c^2 = ab, so cosC = 1/2 and C = 60 deg.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q8 (T.U. 2054, HSEB 2053); book p188 = PDF p215 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: cosA/a = cosB/b becomes sinB*cosA = sinA*cosB, i.e. sin(B-A) = 0.
questions.question: Q9. If the cosines of two of the angles of a triangle are proportional to the opposite sides, prove that the triangle is isosceles.
questions.solution: Suppose cosA/a = cosB/b (the same argument works for any pair). Then b*cosA = a*cosB, i.e. 2R*sinB*cosA = 2R*sinA*cosB, so sinB*cosA - sinA*cosB = sin(B-A) = 0. With angles in (0, pi), B - A = 0, so A = B and the triangle is isosceles.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q9; book p188 = PDF p215 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Either cosA = 0 (right-angled) or the sine factors force B = C: factor, never divide blindly.
questions.question: Q10. If (cosA + 2cosC):(cosA + 2cosB) = sinB:sinC, prove that the triangle is either isosceles or right-angled.
questions.solution: Cross-multiplying: (cosA + 2cosC)*sinC = (cosA + 2cosB)*sinB, i.e. cosA*(sinC - sinB) = 2*(sinB*cosB - sinC*cosC) = sin2B - sin2C. Now sin2B - sin2C = 2*cos(B+C)*sin(B-C) = -2*cosA*sin(B-C), and sinC - sinB = 2*cos((B+C)/2)*sin((C-B)/2) = 2*sin(A/2)*sin((C-B)/2). So 2*cosA*sin(A/2)*sin((C-B)/2) = -2*cosA*sin(B-C) = 4*cosA*sin((C-B)/2)*cos((C-B)/2). If cosA = 0 then A = 90 deg (right-angled). Otherwise divide by 2*cosA*sin((C-B)/2) (zero only if B = C, isosceles): sin(A/2) = 2*cos((C-B)/2). But |(C-B)/2| < (B+C)/2 = (pi-A)/2 gives cos((C-B)/2) > cos((pi-A)/2) = sin(A/2), so 2*cos((C-B)/2) > sin(A/2) always and this case never occurs. Hence B = C (isosceles) or A = 90 deg (right-angled).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q10; book p188 = PDF p215 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: 2*sinC*cosA = sinB expands to sin(C-A) = 0 via sinB = sin(A+C).
questions.question: Q11. If 2cosA = sinB/sinC, show that the triangle is isosceles.
questions.solution: 2*sinC*cosA = sinB = sin(A+C) = sinA*cosC + cosA*sinC. Subtracting cosA*sinC: sinC*cosA = sinA*cosC, i.e. sinC*cosA - sinA*cosC = sin(C-A) = 0. With angles in (0, pi), C = A, so the triangle is isosceles.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q11; book p188 = PDF p215 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Translate both sides to cos2: the condition becomes cos2A + cos2C = 2cos2B, the AP condition.
questions.question: Q12. Prove that a^2, b^2, c^2 are in A.P. if sinA:sinC = sin(A-B):sin(B-C).
questions.solution: a^2, b^2, c^2 in A.P. means 2*sin^2B = sin^2A + sin^2C (dividing by 4R^2), i.e. (1-cos2B) = (1-cos2A)/2 + (1-cos2C)/2, i.e. cos2A + cos2C = 2cos2B. The given condition: sinA*sin(B-C) = sinC*sin(A-B). Left: [cos(A-B+C) - cos(A+B-C)]/2 = [cos(pi-2B) - cos(pi-2C)]/2 = (cos2C - cos2B)/2. Right: [cos(C-A+B) - cos(C+A-B)]/2 = [cos(pi-2A) - cos(pi-2B)]/2 = (cos2B - cos2A)/2. Equality gives cos2C - cos2B = cos2B - cos2A, i.e. cos2A + cos2C = 2cos2B, exactly the A.P. condition.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q12 (condition continues on book p188); book p188 = PDF pp215-216 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: a^2+b^2+c^2 = 4R^2*(sum sin^2) = 8R^2*(1 + cosA*cosB*cosC): the 8R^2 forces a zero cosine.
questions.question: Q14. If 8R^2 = a^2 + b^2 + c^2, prove that the triangle is right angled. (T.U. 2057S)
questions.solution: a^2 + b^2 + c^2 = 4R^2*(sin^2A + sin^2B + sin^2C). Since sin^2A + sin^2B + sin^2C = 2 + 2*cosA*cosB*cosC (standard identity), this equals 8R^2*(1 + cosA*cosB*cosC). Setting it equal to 8R^2 gives cosA*cosB*cosC = 0, so one angle is 90 deg: the triangle is right angled.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q14 (T.U. 2057S); book p188 = PDF p215-216 (vision read)
